4.1

Maximum and Minimum Values

Where is a function biggest and smallest?

Problem

A delivery drone flies a test route. Its altitude is h(t)=t3−12t2+36t+10 metres for 1≤t≤7 seconds. When is it highest, and when is it lowest?

Your instinct may say “look where the graph is flat.” That’s half of the answer. Use the figure below: change the time interval and watch which points win.

Absolute vs. local Definition

f(c) is the absolute maximum of f on D if f(c)≥f(x) for every x in D. It is a local maximum if f(c)≥f(x) for every x near c, meaning on some open interval around c. Minimums are the same with ≤.

Picture a mountain range. The local maxima are hilltops. The absolute maximum is the highest point of the whole range, which might be a hilltop or might be the edge of the map (an endpoint).

Extreme Value Theorem Theorem

If f is continuous on a closed interval [a,b], then f attains an absolute maximum value and an absolute minimum value somewhere in [a,b].

Both conditions matter. 1/x on (0,1] is continuous but has no maximum: the interval is open at 0. A function with a jump can also “aim” for a value it never reaches.

Fermat’s Theorem Theorem

If f has a local maximum or minimum at c, and f′(c) exists, then f′(c)=0.

At the top of a smooth hill the tangent is level. If it tilted, you could step uphill. The converse is false: x3 has f′(0)=0 but no extreme there.

Critical number Definition

A number c in the domain of f where f′(c)=0 or f′(c) does not exist. Local extremes can only happen at critical numbers.

The Closed Interval Method Procedure

To find the absolute max and min of a continuous f on [a,b]:

  1. Find the values of f at the critical numbers in (a,b).
  2. Find f(a) and f(b).
  3. The largest of these values is the absolute maximum; the smallest is the absolute minimum.
Worked example

Find the absolute maximum and minimum of f(x)=x2/3(x−5) on [−1,4].

  1. Rewrite as f(x)=x5/3−5x2/3. Then f′(x)=35​x2/3−310​x−1/3=3x1/35x−10​=3x1/35(x−2)​.
  2. Critical numbers: f′(x)=0 at x=2, and f′ does not exist at x=0. Both are in (−1,4).
  3. Evaluate: f(−1)=1⋅(−6)=−6, f(0)=0, f(2)=−334​≈−4.76, f(4)=−316​≈−2.52.
  4. Absolute max 0 at x=0, a cusp where f′ does not exist. Absolute min −6 at the endpoint x=−1. Neither answer came from solving f′=0.
Your turn

  1. Answer the drone problem: when is the drone highest and lowest on 1≤t≤7?

    Solution

    h′(t)=3t2−24t+36=3(t−2)(t−6), so the critical numbers are t=2 and t=6.

    h(1)=35, h(2)=42, h(6)=10, h(7)=17. Highest: 42 m at t=2 s. Lowest: 10 m at t=6 s.

  2. Find the absolute extreme values of f(x)=x3−3x2−9x+2 on [−2,4].

    Solution

    f′(x)=3x2−6x−9=3(x−3)(x+1); critical numbers −1 and 3.

    f(−2)=0, f(−1)=7, f(3)=−25, f(4)=−18. Max 7 at x=−1; min −25 at x=3.

  3. Find all critical numbers of g(t)=t2/3(t−10).

    Solution

    g′(t)=32​t−1/3(t−10)+t2/3=3t1/32(t−10)+3t​=3t1/35t−20​.

    g′=0 at t=4; g′ undefined at t=0 (which is in the domain). Critical numbers: 0 and 4.

  4. Keep the drone’s start at t=1 and stretch the end time b. For which b does the highest altitude move to the right endpoint?

    Solution

    The endpoint wins once h(b)>42. Solve t3−12t2+36t+10=42: t3−12t2+36t−32=(t−2)2(t−8)=0.

    So h(b)>42 exactly when b>8. Check it in the figure.

Watch out
  • f′(c)=0 doesn’t guarantee an extreme: x3 is flat at 0 but keeps rising.
  • Corners and cusps, where f′ doesn’t exist, are critical numbers too.
  • On a closed interval, always test the endpoints.
  • A critical number must be in the domain. f(x)=1/x has none, even though f′ is undefined at 0.

4.2

The Mean Value Theorem

What does an average rate promise about the instantaneous rate?

Problem

Some highways use average-speed cameras. Two cameras 12 km apart photograph your car 6 minutes apart. Neither camera caught you speeding, yet you get a ticket for 120 km/h in a 100 km/h zone. Is that fair?

Your average speed was 12/0.1=120 km/h. The Mean Value Theorem says that at some instant, your speedometer showed exactly 120.

Rolle’s Theorem Theorem

If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), then there is a number c in (a,b) with f′(c)=0.

Throw a ball up and catch it at the same height. At the top of its flight its vertical velocity is zero.

Mean Value Theorem Theorem

If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), there is a c in (a,b) with f′(c)=b−af(b)−f(a)​,i.e.f(b)=f(a)+f′(c)(b−a).

Tilt Rolle’s picture. Some tangent is parallel to the secant: at some moment, the instantaneous rate equals the average rate.

Why it matters Consequences

  • Zero derivative means constant. If f′(x)=0 for all x in an interval, f is constant there. So if f′=g′ on an interval, then f=g+C. This is exactly why every antiderivative has the form F(x)+C (Section 4.9).
  • Speed limits give distance limits. If ∣f′(x)∣≤M, then ∣f(b)−f(a)∣≤M∣b−a∣. Knowing how fast something can change tells you how far it can get.
  • Counting roots. If f′ is never zero, f can’t have two roots: Rolle would put a zero of f′ between them.
Worked example

Verify the Mean Value Theorem for f(x)=x3−2x on [−1,2] and find every c it promises.

  1. Hypotheses: f is a polynomial, so it is continuous and differentiable everywhere.
  2. Secant slope: 2−(−1)f(2)−f(−1)​=34−1​=1.
  3. Solve f′(c)=3c2−2=1: c2=1, so c=±1.
  4. Only c=1 lies in the open interval (−1,2). c=−1 is an endpoint, so it doesn’t count. Select x3−2x in the figure and set a=−1, b=2 to see it.
Your turn

  1. Find the number c promised by the MVT for f(x)=x​ on [1,9].

    Solution

    Secant slope =9−13−1​=41​. Solve 2c​1​=41​: c​=2, c=4.

  2. For f(x)=1/x on [−1,1], the secant slope is 1, but f′(x)=−1/x2<0 everywhere. Why isn’t this a counterexample to the MVT?

    Solution

    f is not continuous on [−1,1]; it isn’t even defined at 0. A hypothesis fails, so the theorem promises nothing.

  3. Suppose 2≤f′(x)≤4 for all x and f(1)=5. What values can f(4) take?

    Solution

    f(4)=f(1)+f′(c)⋅3 for some c. Since 2≤f′(c)≤4: 5+6≤f(4)≤5+12, so 11≤f(4)≤17.

  4. Show that 2x−1−sinx=0 has exactly one real root.

    Solution

    At least one: f(0)=−1<0 and f(π)=2π−1>0. By the IVT there is a root in (0,π).

    At most one: f′(x)=2−cosx≥1>0. Two roots would force f′(c)=0 between them (Rolle), which is impossible.

Watch out
  • The MVT says c exists. It doesn’t say where, and there may be more than one.
  • c must be strictly between a and b.
  • Check both hypotheses: continuous on the closed interval, differentiable on the open one.

4.3

How Derivatives Affect the Shape of a Graph

What do f′ and f′′ say about the curve?

Problem

A rumour spreads through a school of 1000 students. After t hours, N(t)=1+99e−0.5t1000​ students have heard it. The count only ever goes up. But when is the rumour spreading fastest, the moment the curve stops getting steeper and starts levelling off?

“Rising” is about f′. “Getting steeper” is about f′′. This section connects the signs of both derivatives to the picture.

Increasing/Decreasing Test Test

If f′(x)>0 on an interval, f is increasing there. If f′(x)<0, f is decreasing.

Why: by the MVT, f(x2​)−f(x1​)=f′(c)(x2​−x1​), which has the sign of f′.

First Derivative Test Test

Let c be a critical number of a continuous f.

  • f′ changes +→− at c: local max.
  • f′ changes −→+ at c: local min.
  • No sign change: no local extreme.

Concavity Definition & test

f is concave upward on I if its graph lies above all its tangent lines on I (it holds water), and concave downward if it lies below them.

Test: f′′>0 on I ⇒ concave up. f′′<0 ⇒ concave down.

An inflection point is a point on a continuous curve where the concavity changes.

Second Derivative Test Test

Suppose f′′ is continuous near c and f′(c)=0.

  • f′′(c)>0: local min (flat and cupped up).
  • f′′(c)<0: local max (flat and cupped down).
  • f′′(c)=0: no conclusion. Use the First Derivative Test.
You seeIt meansOn the graph
f′>0f increasingrising left to right
f′<0f decreasingfalling
f′ changes signlocal max or mintop of a hill / bottom of a valley
f′′>0f′ increasing, concave upslope is growing (∪)
f′′<0f′ decreasing, concave downslope is shrinking (∩)
f′′ changes signinflection pointwhere f′ is at a local max or min
Worked example

For f(x)=x5−5x3, find where f increases and decreases, its local extremes, its concavity, and its inflection points. (It’s a preset in the figure.)

  1. f′(x)=5x4−15x2=5x2(x2−3). Critical numbers: 0 and ±3​≈±1.73.
  2. Sign of f′: the factor 5x2≥0, so the sign comes from x2−3. Positive for ∣x∣>3​, negative for 0<∣x∣<3​. So f increases on (−∞,−3​) and (3​,∞) and decreases on (−3​,3​).
  3. First Derivative Test: local max f(−3​)=63​≈10.4; local min f(3​)=−63​. At x=0, f′ is negative on both sides: no extreme, just a flat spot.
  4. f′′(x)=20x3−30x=10x(2x2−3), zero at 0 and ±3/2​≈±1.22. It changes sign at each one.
  5. Concave down on (−∞,−3/2​) and (0,3/2​); concave up on (−3/2​,0) and (3/2​,∞). Three inflection points: x=−3/2​,0,3/2​.
  6. Cross-check with the Second Derivative Test: f′′(3​)=303​>0, a min. At 0, f′′(0)=0, so that test is silent there. That’s why the sign chart of f′ is the more reliable tool.
Your turn

  1. Solve the rumour problem. When is the rumour spreading fastest, and how many students know it at that moment? Hint: you can check that N′=0.5N(1−1000N​).

    Solution

    N′=0.5N(1−N/1000) is a downward parabola in N, largest when N=500. That is the inflection point of N(t): before it the curve gets steeper, after it the curve levels off.

    N=500 when 1+99e−0.5t=2, i.e. e−0.5t=991​, so t=2ln99≈9.19 hours, when 500 students know.

    Choose the rumour preset in the figure to see f′′ cross zero there.

  2. Analyse f(x)=xe−x: increasing/decreasing, extremes, concavity, inflection point.

    Solution

    f′(x)=(1−x)e−x: increasing on (−∞,1), decreasing on (1,∞); local (and absolute) max f(1)=1/e.

    f′′(x)=(x−2)e−x: concave down on (−∞,2), concave up on (2,∞). Inflection point (2,2e−2).

  3. True or false: if f′′(c)=0, then f has an inflection point at c.

    Solution

    False. f(x)=x4 has f′′(0)=0, but f′′=12x2≥0 on both sides, so the curve is concave up throughout. Choose the x4 preset to see it.

Watch out
  • f′′(c)=0 alone doesn’t make an inflection point; the sign of f′′ has to change.
  • The Second Derivative Test is silent when f′′(c)=0. Fall back on the First Derivative Test.
  • In sign charts, squared factors like (x−1)2 never change sign.

Indeterminate Forms and L’Hospital’s Rule

What is 0/0, really?

Problem

Which is bigger for huge x: x10 or ex? At x=10: 1010 against e10≈22026. At x=30, x10 is still about 55 times bigger. Who wins in the end?

The question is limx→∞​x10/ex, an ∞/∞ form. Plugging in tells you nothing. L’Hospital’s Rule settles it.

L’Hospital’s Rule Theorem

Suppose f and g are differentiable and g′(x)=0 near a (except possibly at a), and limx→a​g(x)f(x)​ has the form 00​ or ∞∞​. Then x→alim​g(x)f(x)​=x→alim​g′(x)f′(x)​ provided the limit on the right exists (or is ±∞). It also works for one-sided limits and for x→±∞.

Why, for 0/0: near a, f(x)≈f′(a)(x−a) and g(x)≈g′(a)(x−a). The factors (x−a) cancel, leaving f′(a)/g′(a). Differentiate the top and bottom separately; this is not the Quotient Rule.

FormExampleStrategy
00​, ∞∞​limx→0​xsin3x​Apply the rule directly (maybe more than once).
0⋅∞limx→0+​xlnxRewrite as a quotient: 1/xlnx​.
∞−∞limx→0​(x1​−sinx1​)Common denominator, factor, or multiply by a conjugate.
00, ∞0, 1∞limx→0+​xxTake logs: if y=fg, then lny=glnf. Find limlny=L; the answer is eL.

Growth ladder as x→∞: lnx≪xp≪ex for every power p>0. Logs lose to every power; every power loses to the exponential.

Worked example

(a) x→0lim​x2ex−1−x​   (b) x→0+lim​xx

  1. (a) Plug in: 01−1−0​, form 0/0. Apply the rule: 2xex−1​.
  2. Still 0/0. Apply it again: 2ex​→21​. So the limit is 21​.
  3. (b) Form 00. Let y=xx, so lny=xlnx=1/xlnx​, form ∞−∞​.
  4. L’Hospital: −1/x21/x​=−x→0. So lny→0 and y→e0=1.
Your turn

  1. x→∞lim​x​lnx​

    Solution

    ∞/∞: 1/(2x​)1/x​=x​2​→0.

  2. x→0lim​x3x−sinx​

    Solution

    Three applications: 3x21−cosx​→6xsinx​→6cosx​→61​.

  3. x→∞lim​(1+x3​)2x

    Solution

    Form 1∞. lny=2xln(1+3/x)=1/x2ln(1+3/x)​→2⋅3=6, so y→e6≈403.4. (You can type e^6.)

  4. x→0lim​x+2x+cosx​

    Solution

    It is not indeterminate: plug in to get 21​. Using L’Hospital anyway gives 11−sinx​→1, which is wrong.

  5. x→0lim​(x1​−sinx1​)

    Solution

    Combine: xsinxsinx−x​, form 0/0. Then sinx+xcosxcosx−1​, still 0/0. Then 2cosx−xsinx−sinx​→20​=0.

Watch out
  • Check the form first. The rule only applies to 0/0 and ∞/∞.
  • Differentiate numerator and denominator separately. No Quotient Rule.
  • For 00, ∞0, 1∞, remember to exponentiate at the end.
  • If limf′/g′ doesn’t exist, the rule tells you nothing. limx→∞​xx+sinx​=1, yet 11+cosx​ oscillates.

Summary of Curve Sketching

How do you draw an accurate graph from scratch?

Problem

No calculator. Sketch y=x−1x2​ with every hill, valley, asymptote and bend in the right place.

A table of values can miss all of these. A checklist won’t.

The checklist Guidelines A–H

ADomainWhere is f defined? Watch for zero denominators, even roots, logs.
BInterceptsy-intercept f(0); x-intercepts from f(x)=0 (skip if too hard).
CSymmetryEven f(−x)=f(x); odd f(−x)=−f(x); periodic.
DAsymptotesHorizontal: limx→±∞​f. Vertical: where f→±∞. Slant: lim[f(x)−(mx+b)]=0.
EIncrease / decreaseSign chart of f′.
FLocal max / minWhere f′ changes sign (First Derivative Test).
GConcavity & inflectionSign chart of f′′.
HSketchPlot what you found first, then draw the curve through it.

Slant asymptotes appear for rational functions whose top degree is exactly one more than the bottom degree. Long division gives f(x)=mx+b+denominatorremainder​.

Worked example

Carry out A–H for y=x−1x2​.

  1. A. Domain: all x=1. B. Intercepts: only (0,0). C. No symmetry: f(−x)=−x−1x2​ is neither f(x) nor −f(x).
  2. D. Vertical asymptote x=1: f→+∞ as x→1+, f→−∞ as x→1−. Long division: x−1x2​=x+1+x−11​, so y=x+1 is a slant asymptote. No horizontal asymptote.
  3. E. f′(x)=1−(x−1)21​=(x−1)2x(x−2)​. Increasing on (−∞,0) and (2,∞); decreasing on (0,1) and (1,2).
  4. F. Local max f(0)=0; local min f(2)=4.
  5. G. f′′(x)=(x−1)32​. Concave down for x<1, up for x>1. No inflection point, because x=1 is not in the domain.
  6. H. Two branches: the left one rises to a peak at the origin and dives down the asymptote; the right one comes down from +∞, bottoms out at (2,4), and hugs y=x+1. Step to H in the figure to compare.
Your turn

  1. Sketch y=x4−2x2. Find the extremes and the inflection points.

    Solution

    Even function; x-intercepts 0,±2​. y′=4x(x2−1): local min (±1,−1), local max (0,0).

    y′′=12x2−4: inflection points at x=±3​1​, where y=91​−32​=−95​. Concave up for ∣x∣>3​1​, down between.

  2. Sketch y=x−2x+1​.

    Solution

    Write y=1+x−23​. VA x=2, HA y=1. Intercepts (−1,0) and (0,−21​).

    y′=−(x−2)23​<0: decreasing on each branch, no extremes. y′′=(x−2)36​: concave down for x<2, up for x>2.

  3. For y=xlnx​, find the maximum point. Then check your work with the third preset in the figure.

    Solution

    y′=x21−lnx​, zero at x=e; max value 1/e. y′′=x32lnx−3​ gives an inflection point at x=e3/2≈4.48.

    As x→0+, y→−∞ (VA x=0). As x→∞, y→0 by L’Hospital (HA y=0).

Watch out
  • Cancel common factors before declaring a vertical asymptote. x−1x2−1​ has a hole at 1, not an asymptote.
  • As x→−∞, x2​=∣x∣=−x. Sign errors here create wrong asymptotes.
  • An inflection point must be on the graph. A sign change of f′′ across a vertical asymptote doesn’t count.

4.6

Graphing with Calculus and Technology

What can a picture hide, and how does calculus find it?

Problem

Graph f(x)=x3−0.03x in a standard [−10,10]×[−10,10] window. It looks like it is always increasing. Is it?

A graph only shows what its window can resolve. Calculus tells you where to look.

Calculus + technology Workflow

  1. Graph broadly to see the overall shape.
  2. Compute f′ and f′′ to locate the exact critical numbers and inflection points.
  3. Re-graph on windows chosen to show each feature.

Neither alone is enough. The graph can hide tiny features or very large values; algebra alone can lose the big picture.

Families Idea

A formula with a parameter, like fc​(x)=x4−cx2, describes a whole family of curves. The interesting question: for which c does the shape change?

Shapes usually change when critical numbers merge or disappear: when a discriminant hits zero, or when f′ can no longer change sign.

Worked example

How does the graph of fc​(x)=x4−cx2 depend on c?

  1. fc′​(x)=4x3−2cx=2x(2x2−c).
  2. If c≤0: 2x2−c≥0, so the only critical number is 0, and f′ changes −→+. One minimum, a U shape.
  3. If c>0: critical numbers 0 and ±c/2​. Local max at 0, minima at ±c/2​ with value 4c2​−2c2​=−4c2​. A W shape.
  4. Where do the minima go? At a minimum x2=c/2, so y=−4c2​=−x4. Every minimum point lies on the curve y=−x4.
  5. The shape changes at c=0, where the three critical numbers merge into one.
Your turn

  1. Find the exact local extremes of f(x)=x3−0.03x, and choose a window that shows them.

    Solution

    f′(x)=3x2−0.03=0⇒x=±0.1. Local max f(−0.1)=0.002; local min f(0.1)=−0.002.

    A window like [−0.3,0.3]×[−0.01,0.01] shows both.

  2. For which c does f(x)=x3+cx have two local extremes? For which does it have none?

    Solution

    f′(x)=3x2+c. For c<0: two critical numbers ±−c/3​, a local max and a local min.

    For c≥0: f′≥0, so there are no extremes (at c=0, x=0 is critical but f′ doesn’t change sign).

  3. For which c does f(x)=x2+xc​ have a local minimum with x>0? Where is it?

    Solution

    f′(x)=2x−x2c​=0⇒x3=2c​, which has a positive solution only when c>0.

    Then f′′(x)=2+x32c​>0, so it’s a minimum, at x=3c/2​. For c≤0, f′>0 for all x>0: no minimum there.

Watch out
  • A window can hide features entirely. Let f′ and f′′ tell you where to zoom.
  • For families, find the parameter values where critical numbers merge. That’s where the shape changes.

Optimization Problems

What is the best possible design?

Problem

A drinks company needs a closed cylindrical can holding 1 litre (1000 cm³). Metal is expensive. What radius and height use the least metal? Tall and thin, or short and wide?

A strategy that works Procedure

  1. Understand and draw. What is given? What is to be maximized or minimized?
  2. Name things. Assign variables and write the quantity Q you are optimizing.
  3. Use the constraint to write Q as a function of one variable.
  4. Find the domain of that variable (physical limits).
  5. Calculus: find critical numbers. Confirm max/min with the Closed Interval Method or the test below.
  6. Answer the question that was asked, with units.

First Derivative Test for Absolute Extremes. If c is a critical number of a continuous f on an interval, and f′<0 for all x<c and f′>0 for all x>c, then f(c) is the absolute minimum. The same holds for maxima with the signs reversed. This handles open intervals like r>0.

Worked example · the can

Solve the can problem.

  1. Radius r, height h (cm). Metal = surface area A=2πr2+2πrh (two lids plus the side).
  2. Constraint: πr2h=1000, so h=πr21000​. Substitute: A(r)=2πr2+r2000​, for r>0.
  3. A′(r)=4πr−r22000​=r24(πr3−500)​=0⇒r=3500/π​≈5.42 cm.
  4. A′<0 for smaller r and A′>0 for larger r, so this is the absolute minimum.
  5. h=πr21000​=2r≈10.84 cm, and A≈554 cm². The best can is exactly as tall as it is wide.

Real cans are usually taller than this. The lids are made of thicker metal and the seams cost extra, so the true cost function differs from pure area.

Worked example · the box

Which cut x gives the open box of largest volume?

  1. Base (24−2x)×(24−2x), height x: V(x)=x(24−2x)2, with 0≤x≤12.
  2. V′(x)=(24−2x)2−4x(24−2x)=(24−2x)(24−6x).
  3. Critical numbers: x=4 (and x=12, an endpoint).
  4. Closed Interval Method: V(0)=V(12)=0 and V(4)=4⋅162=1024.
  5. Cut 4 cm squares. The box is 16×16×4 cm with volume 1024 cm³.
Your turn

  1. A farmer has 600 m of fencing to enclose a rectangular field along a straight river. No fence is needed on the river side. What is the largest area?

    Solution

    Sides perpendicular to the river y, parallel side x: x+2y=600. A=y(600−2y), A′=600−4y=0⇒y=150, x=300.

    Maximum area 45000 m². (Endpoints y=0 and y=300 give zero area.)

  2. Find the point on y=x​ closest to (3,0).

    Solution

    Minimize D2=(x−3)2+(x​)2=x2−5x+9 instead of D (same minimizer, easier algebra).

    2x−5=0⇒x=25​. Closest point (25​,5/2​), at distance 211​​≈1.66.

  3. A café sells 300 cups a day at $12 each. Market research says each $1 price cut sells 40 more cups. What price maximizes revenue?

    Solution

    Cut the price by x dollars: R(x)=(12−x)(300+40x)=3600+180x−40x2.

    R′(x)=180−80x=0⇒x=2.25. Price $9.75, selling 390 cups, revenue $3802.50. R′′=−80<0 confirms a maximum.

  4. A rectangle has its base on the x-axis and its top corners on y=12−x2. What is its largest area?

    Solution

    Corners at (±x,12−x2): A=2x(12−x2)=24x−2x3, 0≤x≤12​.

    A′=24−6x2=0⇒x=2; A(2)=4⋅8=32. Endpoints give 0.

Watch out
  • Reduce to one variable before differentiating.
  • Justify max vs. min: endpoints, or the First Derivative Test for absolute extremes.
  • Answer the actual question. Were you asked for the dimensions, the location, or the maximum value?

4.8

Newton’s Method

How do you solve f(x)=0 when there is no formula?

Problem

How does a calculator find 10​? It has no table of square roots. It makes a guess, then improves it, again and again.

Newton’s method turns a reasonable guess into a better one using the tangent line. Each step roughly doubles the number of correct digits.

The formula Method

The tangent at xn​ is y=f(xn​)+f′(xn​)(x−xn​). Setting y=0: xn+1​=xn​−f′(xn​)f(xn​)​. Stop when two successive values agree to the accuracy you need.

For f(x)=x2−10 this becomes xn+1​=21​(xn​+xn​10​): average your guess with 10/guess.

When it fails Cautions

  • f′(xn​)=0: a horizontal tangent never meets the axis.
  • f′(xn​)≈0: the next guess shoots far away, maybe toward a different root.
  • Cycles: x3−2x+2 from x1​=0 bounces 0,1,0,1,…
  • Divergence: for x1/3, every step doubles the error.
nxn​ for 10​, from x1​=3error ∣xn​−10​∣

43.16227766021.5 × 10⁻¹²
Worked example

Solve cosx=x correct to six decimal places.

  1. Rewrite as f(x)=cosx−x=0. Then f′(x)=−sinx−1.
  2. A quick sketch of y=cosx and y=x shows one crossing between 0 and 1. Take x1​=1.
  3. x2​=1−−sin1−1cos1−1​≈0.750364.
  4. x3​≈0.739113, x4​≈0.739085, x5​≈0.739085.
  5. The last two agree to six places: x≈0.739085. (Radians! Check with the cos preset.)
Your turn

  1. Use Newton’s method with x1​=2 to find 39​ to four decimal places.

    Solution

    f(x)=x3−9, xn+1​=xn​−3xn2​xn3​−9​.

    x2​≈2.083333, x3​≈2.080089, x4​≈2.080084. So 39​≈2.0801.

  2. Explain why Newton’s method fails for f(x)=x1/3 from every starting value x1​=0.

    Solution

    xn+1​=xn​−31​xn−2/3​xn1/3​​=xn​−3xn​=−2xn​. Each step flips sides and doubles the distance from the root 0.

  3. ex=3x has a solution between 0 and 1. Find it to four decimal places, starting at x1​=0.5.

    Solution

    f(x)=ex−3x, f′(x)=ex−3.

    x2​≈0.610060, x3​≈0.618997, x4​≈0.619061, x5​≈0.619061. Answer 0.6191.

Watch out
  • Sketch first and pick x1​ close to the root you want.
  • Avoid starting where f′≈0.
  • Trig functions: use radians.
Practice 4.8 →
4.9

Antiderivatives

Given f′, what was f?

Problem

A ball is thrown straight up at 20 m/s from the edge of a roof 25 m above the ground. It misses the roof on the way down. Gravity gives a constant acceleration of −9.8 m/s². How high does it go, and when does it hit the ground?

You know the acceleration but need the position. That means running differentiation backwards, twice.

Antiderivative Definition

F is an antiderivative of f on an interval I if F′(x)=f(x) for all x in I.

All of them at once Theorem

If F is an antiderivative of f on I, the most general antiderivative on I is F(x)+C, where C is an arbitrary constant.

This comes from Section 4.2: two functions with the same derivative on an interval differ by a constant.

Worked example · the ball

Solve the roof problem. Take up as positive and t=0 at the throw.

  1. a(t)=−9.8. Antidifferentiate: v(t)=−9.8t+C. Since v(0)=20, C=20: v(t)=−9.8t+20.
  2. Antidifferentiate again: s(t)=−4.9t2+20t+D. Since s(0)=25, D=25: s(t)=−4.9t2+20t+25.
  3. Top of the flight: v=0 at t=9.820​≈2.04 s. Height s≈45.4 m.
  4. Ground: s(t)=0⇒t=9.820+400+490​​≈5.08 s (reject the negative root). Impact velocity v≈−29.8 m/s.
Worked example · two conditions

Find f if f′′(x)=12x2−6x+2, f(0)=1, f(1)=4.

  1. f′(x)=4x3−3x2+2x+C.
  2. f(x)=x4−x3+x2+Cx+D.
  3. f(0)=D=1. f(1)=1−1+1+C+1=2+C=4⇒C=2.
  4. f(x)=x4−x3+x2+2x+1.
Your turn

  1. Find the most general antiderivative of f(x)=4x3−x2​+5cosx.

    Solution

    F(x)=x4−2ln∣x∣+5sinx+C (separate constants allowed on each side of 0).

  2. Find f if f′(x)=3x2−4x+1 and f(1)=5. Then give f(2).

    Solution

    f(x)=x3−2x2+x+C; f(1)=0+C=5. So f(x)=x3−2x2+x+5 and f(2)=8−8+2+5=7.

  3. A car travelling at 30 m/s brakes with constant deceleration 6 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?

    Solution

    v(t)=30−6t, s(t)=30t−3t2. It stops at t=5 s, after s(5)=150−75=75 m.

  4. Find f if f′(x)=1+x21​ and f(1)=0. What is f(0)?

    Solution

    f(x)=tan−1x+C, and f(1)=4π​+C=0. So f(x)=tan−1x−4π​ and f(0)=−4π​≈−0.785. (You can type -pi/4.)

Watch out
  • Always include +C, then use the initial condition to find it.
  • The power rule fails for x−1; its antiderivative is ln∣x∣.
  • If the domain has gaps, each piece can have its own constant.
